title: Iterators and Generators Quiz
description: Practice lambda, decorators, generators, functools, and itertools.

questions.prompt: What does lambda x: x + 1 create?
questions.explanation: lambda makes a one-expression function without a def name.

questions.prompt: sorted([3, 1, 2], key=lambda x: -x) returns:
questions.explanation: key sorts by negated value, descending order.

questions.prompt: A decorator wraps a function to add behavior before or after it runs.
questions.explanation: Decorators are syntactic sugar for function transformation.

questions.prompt: yield inside a function makes it:
questions.explanation: Calling the function returns a generator object.

questions.prompt: next(gen) on a generator:
options: Runs until the next yield and returns that value
questions.explanation: Generators produce values lazily one step at a time.

questions.prompt: map(lambda x: x**2, [1, 2, 3]) in Python 3 is:
questions.explanation: Use list(map(...)) to materialize all results.

questions.prompt: @functools.lru_cache on a function helps when:
options: The same arguments repeat and results can be reused
questions.explanation: LRU cache stores recent call results to save work.

questions.prompt: itertools.chain([1, 2], [3]) conceptually:
options: Iterates through each iterable in sequence
questions.explanation: chain flattens multiple iterables without building a big list first.

questions.prompt: Generators can save memory compared to building a huge list upfront.
questions.explanation: Lazy iteration produces one item at a time.

questions.prompt: @decorator above def f(): is roughly equivalent to:
questions.explanation: The decorator is applied at function definition time.

questions.prompt: filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, range(5)) keeps:
questions.explanation: filter keeps items where the function returns truthy.

questions.prompt: A generator expression (x for x in range(3)) is like:
questions.explanation: Parentheses make a generator expression instead of a list.

questions.prompt: lambda can contain only a single expression, not statements.
questions.explanation: Use def for multi-line logic.

questions.prompt: functools.partial(func, 2) creates:
options: A new callable with some arguments pre-filled
questions.explanation: partial fixes leading arguments for later calls.

questions.prompt: itertools.count(10) produces:
questions.explanation: count is useful with islice to take a finite prefix.

questions.prompt: def gen(): yield 1; yield 2 — list(gen()) is:
questions.explanation: Consuming the generator collects all yielded values.

questions.prompt: Decorators can be used on functions and classes.
questions.explanation: @ wraps callables or classes depending on what the decorator returns.

questions.prompt: Which is valid for a one-line key function?
questions.explanation: lambda s: len(s) sorts by string length.

questions.prompt: yield from other_gen delegates to:
questions.explanation: yield from forwards yields from a sub-iterator.

questions.prompt: When lambda is overused, readability often improves by:
options: Using a normal def with a clear name
questions.explanation: Named functions document intent better than long lambdas.
